summary: Postmortem follow-up for the 2027-01-08 incident where Kestrel saw elevated tail latency and ~15% errors after a production rollout. Redwood SE identified a suspected kernel/batching regression tied to a quantization patch that caused CPU fallback and cache thrash. Agreement on immediate mitigations (revert and patch), longer-term telemetry and soak testing, and a Dedicated trial to stabilize capacity.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-09
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Evan Liu (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Kestrel SRE), Liam O'Neill (Kestrel CTO), Ravi Kumar (Kestrel Eng Manager)

Summary (auto): interim RCA discussion, mitigation plan, trial and logs requested.

[00:00] Samira: hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate ya making time. quick goal for today is to run through the interim rca and align on next steps for the revert and the soak test, and get kestrel what they need for the dedicated trial.
[00:15] Maya: yep thanks, um we got hit pretty hard last night, tail latency spiked and about 15% of our requests turned 5 03/timeout or partials, so pretty painful for our users.
[00:28] Liam: timeline was about 12:15 UTC we started seeing alerts, peaked at ~12:40, resolved around 15:20 when you rolled the rollback. p95 went from ~180ms to ~2.3s. bad for live search.
[00:45] Evan: thanks, yeah so preliminary look from our side — and quick caveat, still investigating — but we saw a kernel-level fallback triggered by the quantization patch we shipped in the 01/08 deploy. in certain seq-len patterns the optimized attention kernel fell back to a slower path, which increased CPU usage and caused more frequent garbage collect and evictions in the serving nodes.
[01:10] Ravi: when you say fallback, is that like NV fallback to CPU or just slower code path on GPU? we saw gpu utl still high but a bunch of processes were OOMing.
[01:22] Evan: good question. it's not a device-level fallback to CPU host execution exactly, more a library fallback inside the runtime that chooses a generic kernel (non-quant optimized) when it detects shape/quant corner case. that generic kernel is less memory efficient and increased memory pressure which then led to task evictions by the orchestrator, returning 503s. couple that with higher latency and batching clump effects and you get cascades.
[01:45] Maya: that matches our logs — high eviction counts and a lot of kv cache misses during the window. our caches were thrashing which made the requests hit cold paths more often.
[02:00] Samira: sorry to interrupt, quick clarification — the repo patch you mentioned, is that one we pushed to the model runtime on Friday? and do we have a diff we can share?
[02:10] Evan: yep that's the Friday quant opt. i have an initial diff, i'll share the revert diff and flamegraphs after this call. it's small but it touches the kernel selector heuristics. so immediate mitigation was rollback which brought p95 back to normal.
[02:30] Liam: can you also explain why autoscaler didn't add capacity during the spike? we expected scale-up to cover the load.
[02:40] Evan: looks like two things: scale-up did kick but the scale unit granularity plus the warmup of dedicated containers meant we had a transient window where concurrency increased beyond available tasks. also some nodes were marked unhealthy because of the OOMs and were drained, reducing effective capacity. autoscaler thresholds are currently tuned for cost and were slower than we'd like for these short noisy spikes.
[03:05] Ravi: so is the plan to change autoscaler behavior? bump shorter cooldowns? more reserved capacity?
[03:12] Samira: yes — short-term we recommend enabling a small reserved dedicated pool for your critical routes (we can do a trial), plus adjust autoscaler on staging to use a more aggressive scale-up policy for the next 2 weeks while we bake the kernel fix.
[03:30] Maya: on the data/privacy side, a couple of questions from our security team — were any customer payloads logged to third-party services during the incident? we saw increased logs but need confirmation.
[03:40] Evan: we did not ship payloads externally. the increased logs were internal diagnostics and blob traces in our internal telemetry store. we'll provide the exact log retention entries; we can also redact payloads before sharing if you want copies for your audit.
[03:58] Liam: and SOC2/ISO posture — do you have an updated artifacts link we can send to our compliance folks? they asked overnight.
[04:05] Samira: yes, i'll share the SOC2 Type II report and the security whitepaper. also SSO/SAML and KMS docs. i'll put links in the follow-up mail.
[04:18] Maya: ideal outcome for us is twofold: (1) no regression in tail latency from runtime updates, (2) ability to absorb spikes without user-visible errors. if we can run a soak that reproduces the pattern and prove it stays under target, we'll be comfortable moving forward.
[04:35] Evan: agreed. for the soak we'll run a targeted seq-length distribution and prefix warm cache scenarios to replicate kv-miss storms. we have a tail-runner harness that simulates distribution; propose 24 hours with a canary step at 2h and 6h to check p95/p99 and eviction counts.
[04:55] Ravi: what's the acceptance criteria? p95 < 250ms and error rate < 0.5%? those sound good to us.
[05:05] Samira: sounds reasonable. we'll confirm exact SLAs in the follow-up doc but 250ms p95 and <0.5% error rate during soak is the working goal.
[05:15] Maya: also one ask — can Redwood enable extended tracing for prefix/KV cache hits on staging so we can see where misses come from? gives us better root cause.
[05:25] Evan: yes, we'll enable extended tracing and push the telemetry to a read-only bucket for you. note there will be size/time tradeoffs; we'll keep it to the soak window and then rotate.
[05:40] Liam: about Dedicated trial — what's the minimum commitment? we want to test reserved capacity to see if that prevents the noisy neighbor / scale-up window.
[05:50] Samira: we can do a short Dedicated trial for 30 days with a small reserved pool, special onboarding support and SLA for that window. no long-term commitment required for the trial; if you like it we can convert to a standard reserved capacity agreement.
[06:08] Maya: perfect. from our side we'll need pricing and an onboarding checklist.
[06:12] Samira: i'll send both today along with SOC2 and the interim RCA notes.
[06:20] Evan: last technical note — we believe there's also an edge case in the quant selector that only pops up when you have mixed quant and fp models in the same serving group and with a particular prefix distribution; we'll run an A/B on staging to validate fix covers it.
[06:40] Ravi: ok, and once you have the revert diff and flamegraphs we'll schedule a shorter technical deep dive for our engineers if needed.
[06:48] Samira: yep, let's tentatively plan that for 2027-01-12 (tech deep dive) if the team is ready. we'll confirm in the follow-up mail.
[06:55] Liam: thanks everyone. one more thing — can you also include a list of request ids we should search for in our logs so we can cross-check? that would help.
[07:05] Evan: i'll include a mapping and the request id ranges for the incident window.
[07:12] Samira: great — to recap: Evan share interim RCA + diffs by 1/11; Maya share logs by 1/10; Samira send Dedicated trial doc + SOC2 by 1/13; Redwood infra run 24h soak starting 1/14 and share results; follow-up sync 1/18. action items noted.
[07:30] Maya: thanks, appreciate the responsiveness. we'll review materials and flag anything else. good call.
[07:38] Samira: thanks all, we'll follow up via email and drop links. end call.
